title: Phishing & Cyber-Security Awareness
blurb: Spotting scam emails, texts and calls, and the habits that keep our systems and supplier payments safe.
siteNotes: Who to report a suspicious message to on each shift, and how
Who is allowed to approve changes to supplier bank details, and the known phone number used to check them
legalNotes: No regulation is stated in the trainer. Good practice only.

cards.title: Phishing & Cyber-Security Awareness
cards.body:
By the end of this session you can:
- say what phishing is and spot the warning signs
- follow the golden rules for links, passwords and payments
- report anything suspicious straight away

cards.title: It starts with a person
cards.body:
Most cyber-attacks on a business do not start with a genius hacker. They start with a scam message that tricks a person.

This is called phishing: an email, text or call pretending to be someone trustworthy (a bank, a supplier, even the boss).

items.title: Infect
items.text: Get you to open something that infects our systems

cards.title: If it feels off, it probably is

items.title: Payment request
items.text: To change bank details or send money

cards.title: Links, passwords, payments
cards.body:
Do not click links or open attachments you were not expecting.

Never enter your password after following a link in a message.

Always verify a request to change bank details or make a payment by contacting the person a different way, such as a known phone number, not by replying. Fraudsters love to redirect supplier payments this way.

left.title: Do
items: Lock your screen when you step away

right.title: Do not
items: Reply to verify a payment change

cards.title: Even if you already clicked
cards.body:
Report anything suspicious to your manager straight away, even if you already clicked.

Fast reporting lets us limit any damage.

> When in doubt, do not click. Ask.

cards.title: Remember
cards.body:
- Phishing is a scam message pretending to be someone trustworthy
- Urgency, odd links, attachments and payment requests are warning signs
- Verify bank detail changes a different way, never by replying
- Never share passwords; lock your screen
- Report straight away, even if you clicked

options: A scam message pretending to be someone trustworthy
A way of backing up important files
A fault that makes the till run slowly
A check that confirms a guest's booking
cards.why: Phishing is an email, text or call pretending to be someone trustworthy, to steal passwords or money or infect our systems.

cards.q: A sense of urgency is a common sign of a phishing message.
cards.why: "Act now or else" is one of the classic warning signs.

cards.q: You get an unexpected email with a link. You should:
options: Click it to check where it goes
Not click it, and verify or report it
Forward it to guests as a warning
Reply and ask the sender to confirm
cards.why: Do not click links you were not expecting. Verify another way or report it.

cards.q: You should verify any request to change bank details by contacting the person a different way.
cards.why: Verify through a known phone number, not by replying. Fraudsters love to redirect supplier payments.

cards.q: Which of these is a warning sign of a phishing message?
options: A greeting by your first name
A reply to a booking you made
A sender address that is slightly wrong
A message sent during working hours
cards.why: Warning signs include urgency, an unexpected link or attachment, a sender address that is slightly wrong, poor spelling and requests to change payment details.

cards.q: It is fine to share your password with a colleague if they ask.
If you think you clicked something suspicious, you should:
options: Say nothing and hope it is fine
Report it to your manager straight away
Delete your emails to cover your tracks
Restart your computer and carry on
cards.why: Report it straight away, even if you already clicked. Fast reporting lets us limit any damage.

cards.q: You should lock your screen when you step away.
cards.why: Locking your screen when you step away is one of the everyday habits.

options: Supplier payments
The lunch menu
Staff rotas
Guest check-ins
cards.why: Fraudsters love to redirect supplier payments by asking you to change bank details.

cards.q: When in doubt about a message, the safest thing is to ask rather than click.
cards.why: When in doubt, do not click. Ask.
